**@NafahatAuliya** (👍20 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0qEHuyTTp8&lc=Ugz61TSt6W9_ZBWbJrN4AaABAg
  The methods are:
  1. Input:
   Reading fiction to understand people and their perspective
  2. Output:
  Writing to improve, modify and learn from mistakes 
  3. Pacing:
  Listening music and movies to catch the natural flow of the language and slang
  4. Mimicking: 
  Speaking like the natives
  
  BONUS: 
  1. Flash cards
  a. Write the meaning
  b. Write a sentence
  c. Write the phonetics
  d. Draw a picture 
  2. Envelope 
  Make a sentence using that word
  
  Homework:
  Practice one method each day and take a day off and repeat

  Thanks for the excellent video James! My way to improve my speaking is mimicking when watching a video (just like this one). I put subtitle and I pause each part before he speaks and I try to speak the phrase after I check if I spoke correctly with the same pacing, intonation... 
  Of course, the video will take longer, but you also will absorb much more the lesson that you are watching and practice your output. 
  
  
  During watching a video:
  Pause each part - Read and speak the subtitle
  Resume - Listen and check you if said correctly
  Pause again if necessary - say again with the same pacing

  Can you help us how to use "due", "due on", "due by" and "due for"? I cannot barely recognize the difference between them. Thank you.
    ↳ **@PlotTwistEnglish** (👍0 · 2020-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VZ87Ofx4eKs&lc=UgwOay7W664xgig6yDN4AaABAg.95a3ogkWEVo96JnVKAvL_w
      due = to be planned or expected for a certain date
      
      
      due on = to be expected on, or planned for, a specific day or date (eg. due on Monday)
      due for = expected or planned for a certain date or day (same as DUE ON)
      due by = expected for a certain date, you can use it with a general time, (eg. due by next week)

      Hi Michael, In my opinion, "Try not to laugh" is grammatically correct. The verb is "To laugh", there is no verb "To not laugh". We say "To not laugh" socially, as a clear and specific challenge to keep a straight (non-laughing) face. Hope that helps! Tony

    ↳ **@MazzixG** (👍0 · 2020-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S7Q3XP7nvj4&lc=UgxaDEo0Di40MeWKgj14AaABAg.90NDoJZifvn90P4hQZ6R9Z
      To have is an irregular verb that means owing sth .. 
      Have in present simple doesn't change in these subjects  ( I you we you they) but (s/he it ) have becomes has so we say : 
      I have a dog
      You have a dog
      She/he/it has a dog
      You have a dog
      They have a dog 
      But in  past simple and past participle have changes to had 
      And it's used for the all the subjects 
      I/ you /she/he/it/we/you/they  .. had a dog ( in past simple )
      There are many videos that explain this so you can  check them out 
      Good luck

  At 13:00, there is the sentence "Mr. E is happy because he knew Raquel would come if he would let her cook dinner." But in school, we learned that the word "would" is never a part of an if-clause. So, who is right? It would be nice to know because I'm writing my final exam (German Abitur) this year. Thanks for your help
    ↳ **@VictorMatthieu** (👍0 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B3Xd5FRBEx4&lc=Ugz01x2XkTPpDc0fwBF4AaABAg.9-s2ZEk8e739E5qMW1H0Jd
      I'm American. It sounds fine to me. I don't know if there's any sort of special grammar rule, but I've said it before. To me, it sounds extra conditional. Typically I would use it with the perfect aspect and/or probably also with the word "only", rather than just having "would" by itself. So, something like this:
      
      ". . . if only he'd have let her cook dinner." / ". . . if only he'd let her cook dinner." / ". . . if he'd have let her cook dinner."
      
      Those sound more natural to me. But, like I said, I don't know if there's some grammar rule that bans this, but honestly, most "rules" English don't really mean much and language is a very dynamic thing so you can't really usually say something is or isn't allowed. Plus with all the dialects of English (and there are A LOT), I'm sure it also depends on what type of English you're studying.

    ↳ **@VictorMatthieu** (👍0 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B3Xd5FRBEx4&lc=Ugx7eZAV8s7RAHEt3594AaABAg.90Jb85g4e5N9J5CDFZdNeb
      If there is a modal verb, you use its opposite (had -> hadn't; would -> wouldn't; will -> won't; etc). When there's no modal, you use "do". Keep the tense the same. 
      
      Your sentence is past with no modal and it's a positive statement.
      
      This means we will use "didn't"
      
      Did -> because it's a past tense main clause with no modal
      
      n't -> because the main clause is positive

      This structure is much less common as it can only be used with non-count or uncountable nouns (such as water, oxygen, philosophy). The article must be omitted when the non-count noun is used as an open generalisation. 
      Examples :
      All water is wet.
      I want all alcohol removed from this school.
      All sport is good for you.

      Sorry, but this isn't a great summary. The key takeaway is missing, which was that speaking and listening are good to reinforce words you already know, but if you don't know a word you obviously won't say it and you also won't understand it. Whereas reading forces you and allows you to pause, look up the word, and add it to your vocabulary. You can do this at a surface level, only looking up words that prevent your understanding, or you can do it intensively, whereby you actively study a text sentence by sentence, study it's makeup and structure and then cover it up and re-create it from memory.
    ↳ **@DeShark88** (👍0 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=Ugwwhi3tjQA4Nr1tF-B4AaABAg.9lhvoLscbPyA3k_4iVzs21
      All the stuff about lingq, or however it's spelt, was to show you that importing ebooks allows you to very easily use the online dictionary to define words you don't know. Whereas some languages (like Chinese) has awful dictionaries where finding definitions is a slog, online learning permits rapid look-ups which makes learning more fun, which makes learning more likely.

**@GandalfTheWise0002** (👍14 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=Ugwx8rOCY8rsbrj6p6R4AaABAg
  I've found that combination of intensive and extensive reading effective as well.  In addition, I do something partway in between I think of as targeted reading.  If there is a particular aspect of the language that is frustrating me when I run across it, I target it each time I encounter it until it is not frustrating.  The first time I tried it, I had hit a plateau in Ancient Greek in my extensive reading.   I had improved quite a bit, but just seemed to not get any better.  Intensive reading wasn't effectively fixing this either.   It was an issue of internalizing grammar to the point it was automatic.
  
   I don't remember why, but I decided to fix one problem at a time.  The first obvious problem was that I hadn't internalized verb endings of the indicative cases to the point they were completely automatic.  To fix this, during extensive reading, I paused at each indicative (and subjunctive verb), thought about it intentionally for a bit, then picked up again with extensive reading at the beginning of that sentence.  I found that quick emphasis on a particular aspect of the language helped internalize it.  Within a few days, the verb endings were not much of a problem so I stopped focusing on them.
  
  I've found that this targeting of the aspect of grammar that is most annoying and frustrating applies the Pareto Principle to clearing out the worst stumbling blocks to comfortable extensive reading.  I don't stay on one aspect until I have it perfect, but rather until it's not a noticeable impediment to smooth extensive reading.   This is something that is much like what using parallel texts, interlinears, or computer click-for-definition functions is for vocabulary when extended reading, except it's for grammar.  It's a momentary distraction to the reading, but gives a quick  review on what is needed.   
  
  I found targeted reading a great addition to both intensive and extensive reading.  It's a minor temporary slowdown to extended reading that gives a permanent bump up in skills.  I've found that this targeting usually clears most stumbling blocks in a few days or at most a week without turning all my reading time into intensive reading.

  Trying to learn Polish, reading children's books. Way more difficult than it is implied here to improve my vocab by just reading the books. **@nathanlaoshi8074** (👍2 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=UgwatajV8jnawIcWn2Z4AaABAg
  Problems with looking up every unknown word:  1) it takes forever, 2) you might "guess" the wrong meaning for words with multiple definitions, and 3) it makes the entire exercise very disjointed.  This is where Krashen comes in:  if you have a mostly comprehensible text, context will help the student "guess" more accurately than looking up the word, and the flow is maintained.  Of course, you have a limited selection that way, and if the content is not compelling enough, motivation to power through is tough to come by.
  
  Personally, I prefer a hybrid approach:  I read whatever the heck I feel like reading, ignore most of the unknown vocab (many words will become clear enough with time), and only look up words used in at least five instances where I think meaning is being obscured by not knowing them.  This technique worked for me in French, German, and Italian, and is working just fine in Spanish.  Mandarin is more challenging; I have yet to arrive at a technique for that one.
    ↳ **@saikougenz** (👍0 · 2025-12-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=UgwatajV8jnawIcWn2Z4AaABAg.9tPdGeCPCh_AQUoEriTanl
      but you have to start somewhere, so it’s fine for beginners to keep look things up until they reach a level where they can infer the meaning of a word from surrounding words and context.

  Is it normal while I'm using LingQ to read a text and mark too many words as yellow LingQ? I recently read a text and I'm frustrating because of it, sounds like that I don't even know nothing if I compare directly to Ankis monolingual's method of taking a sentence with just one unknown word to evolve it
    ↳ **@Thelinguist [channel author]** (👍2 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=UgyqdUzrrOB-SQVshAp4AaABAg.9l_9eVC1xW79l_OwJNwxV2
      When I begin there are lots of blue words which become yellow. Since I start with the mini-stories, there is so much repetition that many become white (known). As I progress into more difficult material there are fewer blue words, altho at least 10-15%. But this also improves. Yellow words should gradually convert to white because you see them so often or move them manually to known.
    ↳ **@anaxluisa** (👍1 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=UgyqdUzrrOB-SQVshAp4AaABAg.9l_9eVC1xW79lbMl_pAomq
      That's totally normal, especially if you're learning a language from scratch! People go about it differently, but as Steve mentioned, once you repeat the lessons and progress through them, you can manually change the level of yellow words (from 1 to 4), so they will gradually become white.
      
      I started Korean on LingQ from a lower beginner level with the Mini Stories, and I would say 95+% of the words I read where yellow in any given lesson, but as I continued moving forward and complementing that study with reading from other courses in a similar difficulty stage as well, I quickly started seeing that number decrease as I got exposed to the same words over and over again.
      
      Again, people go about it differently, but I change the number on a yellow word every time I can guess the meaning, so they gradually become white. If at some point I can't recall it that's not a big deal, I just move it back to yellow. The important thing is to keep reading from different materials at a similar level, because that way you get exposed to both new and repeated words, and that makes it easier to understand new blue words through context. After two months, most of what I read went from 95% to 55% new words, which is a massive improvement. I can now (very slowly) read webtoons, which was inconceivable when I started with the language.

      "Habits are like the atoms of our lives. Each one is a fundamental unit that contributes to your overall improvement.     ↳ **@Rudolphhhhhh** (👍1 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=UgzY0BFJMbuIJWsp4uB4AaABAg.9l_zwPgT7RT9laDZtn2UVh
      Nonsense. First of all, Alphonse Daudet is not François Rabelais: aside from some archaic words or sentence structure, at least 90% of the vocabulary and grammar that is used in those short stories, are usable nowadays in French. Then, everyone should know that in each language in the world, the language used in books, even in the new ones, is not really the language that is actually spoken. For example, even today, we are using "passé simple" tense in French novels, but almost never in spoken language. So, it is the learner that has to be clever enough to know that the vocabulary and grammar used in books are not always usable in real life: to know that, he has to vary the different contents of reading (the old ones as well as the new ones) and compare that with the reality of real conversation with French natives (knowing that even among native French people, not everyone speaks the same way, e.g. social network's jargon filled with a lot of invasive English words, or young Arabic native people who are living in the suburbs, this is definitely not the French I speak).
      
      Then, it is like the Japanese language that is spoken in anime: people tend to say that we definitely have to avoid learning Japanese from anime, because it is supposed to be too rude. But it is also a big mistake to think like that, because actually, there are much more usable vocabulary and grammar in those anime that not usable ones. So, it is the learner that has to be clever enough to discover by himself what is actually usable of not in real life without shocking native people, thanks to conversations and diversification of what he reads and listens.
      
      In other words: diversification, diversification, and diversification.

      @Asrashas  Currently I'd say I'm at a low intermediate level in Japanese. My vocab is lacking quite a bit but I know at least 500 kanji, probably closer to 800 or something (I don't really keep track).
      The radicals that make up a kanji can give a clue to its meaning and/or its reading.
      泳 (swim), 注 (pour) and 波 (wave) all have meanings related to water, and all have氵at the side, which is a form of the radical for water.
      The kanji 亡 can be read as ぼう (bou).
      望, 忙 and 忘 all contain 亡 as one their radicals and have ぼう as one of their readings.
      So once you know a decent amount of kanji, it becomes a lot easier to pick others up because of this.
      There have been times where a word had a kanji I didn't know, but I was able to work out the kanji reading based on the radicals. Then when I put together the reading of the whole word, I realised I already knew it, but it was a word I had only heard spoken and never seen written down.
      So yes, you definitely need more knowledge for this in Japanese compared to some other languages, but it's maybe not as bad as you think.
      I think a few hundred kanji would be a good starting point to jump into reading. And you only need to learn the meanings, since it's much better to learn the kanji readings by just learning the words they're used in.

  The biggest problem that I've with a new language is the sound of the letters.
  
  Not to mention not all languages uses latin as base.
  
  Say, I'd be diving on russian or whatnot. 
  IF I learn first the sound of letters, then I can read anything on the screen, answer correctly, and also start practicing my pronunciation from vowel to vowel, letter by letter.
  It's quite a simple concept, when we start in school, this is exactly the very first thing we're exposed to, before we can learn how to write and read, and thus speak.
  
  
  I haven't tried many language tools yet, and definitely haven't given enough time... 
  Duolingo, babbel, talk pal, memrise. 
  
  From those, memrise leagues ahead of anything else. I need to the learn the very foundation, before I can actually learn words.
  For instance, when a tried a new language on duo, I had to memorize word by word, and on top of that, try to also make a memory from the sound of each word... Which is obviously inefficient and dumb. From memrise, it's not required, because I'd get the foundation to "how to read" from the get go. And then I can learn words, without having to memorize each word. I can have a good idea about the pronunciation, without having to practice word by word, because I know how each letter is meant to sound. 
  
  IDK, maybe I am biased, but I just don't get it... Yeah, Talk Pal would get me faster into speaking with natives... But at same time, I'd be a illiterate, not knowing how to write, read and having to waste a lot of time to memorize  word by word. 
  
  I'll give a try to your recommendations but... I think the best case scenario is.
  Memrise for base and foundation, then talk pal or speak (haven't tried) to further practice pronunciation through conversation. Anyways...

**@kalevipoeg6916** (👍0 · 2026-04-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qgUIa-Vbxs8&lc=UgyO9McEcdquu3DEKyB4AaABAg
  Here's the problem with you "trying" 47 language learning tools: 
  because the objective is to see which one leads you to fluency, scientifically speaking the only REAL way of doing that would be to choose dozens of people with roughly the same level of intelligence, same age bracket, similar levels of motivation and focus and to have THEM learn the same language with English as their native tongue (to eliminate the variable of mother tongue making it easier or harder), all of them being monolingual so there's no linguistic cross-pollination going on  - and you have them use the apps for let's say 1 year, every day for a set amount of time with a set number of lessons - so that nobody is spending 5 hours a day while the other guy spends 30 minutes a day which warps results - and from THERE you can can them tested in their proficiency level - reading, writing, listening comprehension and speech output, vocabulary level, etc. - and THEN you can say something useful about the apps. UNTIL then it's all anecdotal at best - "I feel like I gained more from this one". ALSO, if you're learning the same language from multiple apps, you've already tainted your results because even a LITTLE bit of learning from one makes it harder to gage the results of the other. 
  
  My suggestion is, maybe constrain it to the top dozen language learning tools, find a couple dozen volunteers willing to do this with you (some WILL drop out along the way, humans are like that, so backups are necessary) and get a baseline on them as monolinguals with a DESIRE to learn language but no experience in actually doing so, and follow up with them - maybe even add incentives if they make it the full year and make sure they're ONLY doing the app and nothing else, for a set amount of learning time each day. 
  
  THEN you compare the results with the SAME language and the same MOTHER tongue - English, let's say, learning Chinese, a VERY distant language. 
  
  The added complication is that even within the same program different language courses may have different results just depending on how that method clicks for each person but it's a START. 
  
  I'd love to see a video from you in a year or so with exactly this kind of experiment - because that's ACTUALLY valuable data.

  Absolutely! I'm doing a lot of reading now in Spanish (I've been using the Dreaming Spanish method of listening). I probably should've started reading much earlier since I'm hearing impaired, and it's harder for me to follow fast Spanish, or pick up words being used. 
  
  I've spent 5 1/2 months so far of intensive reading, and not only has my reading stamina gone up, I've been noticing tons of little words throughout each book. Including escalofrío (like the French equivalent in the video). Even noticing grammar tenses have become much, much easier. The le/se/me/te words before/after a conjugated verb aren't confusing me as much, and I'm starting to pick out root words too, but only if I read it slowly. Although, the funny thing about reading C1/C2 level books is, I'll sometimes come across a word in Spanish and when Iook up the meaning in English, it's some obscure word I've never heard of, or it's the same obscure word. I've seen 2 like this in a C1 level book I'm reading right now. For the B1/B2 level books I'm reading, I'm really starting to notice that snowball effect.
  
  On the speaking part, I've been trying that more. I'm 49, so I'm kind of old-school, and there's that old habit that's like, "If I don't have correct, proper grammar, the whole thing will be marked wrong!". But, I'll try to say something and check it, and it'll be on the right track (maybe an accent was off, or a tense was off, or words were re-ordered). One thing that I'm probably going to try and do is, after reading a paragraph of a book, try to describe the gist out loud in basic Spanish (A2/B1 level).
  
  With the C1/C2 level "challenge books" as I call them (yeah, maybe 20% of words are unknown), I'll read 1 chapter without looking anything up, seeing what I can make of the gist, then I look at a translation of the chapter, then I go through a paragraph or two slowly to pick out words I've seen occuring a few times (lately, I've been trying to describe the word using simple Spanish), then re-read that paragraph without stopping. I liken it to a video game where you're fighting a tough final boss or a tricky level. The first time, it might take 4 hours, then you look up how to beat it (i.e., the translation), then play it again, and your brain is like, "Ah yes, I remember you! You did X and Y and I need to do A and B". Only with reading it's like, "Ah yes, I remember escalofrío from that previous book! So, this must be a tense/uneasy situation the character is going through".
  
  With flashcards, the only time I've ever used them was 26 years ago learning Kanji (Tuttle Kanji Cards), but I would also say the kanji out loud, too. Personally, my ideal flash card would be:
  
  Front: TL word. 3-5 comprehensible sentences.
  Back: (bold, white text) Definition of the word in A2/B1 level (or 1 level below the word's CEFR level). Personal note (small font, blue text) to give me a hint. Same background/foreground answer (for a spoiler text) containing the English word.

**@user-albsim** (👍1 · 2026-06-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJBP34upuAM&lc=UgxOxdeyMPWXAr5ga6B4AaABAg
  For what it’s worth, I think the brain operates in completely different modes when learning vocabulary.
  
  1) Translation mode
  This is common among beginners. A foreign word is mentally translated into the native language before meaning is accessed.
  
  2) Association mode
  At a later stage, the brain begins reinforcing links between words and concepts directly. Meaning becomes connected to images, tastes, experiences, situations, and emotions. Semantic neural networks are gradually built.
  
  3) Chunk mode
  The learner no longer processes language word by word. Entire phrases, sentence patterns, and complex expressions are stored and retrieved as semantic units.
  
  4) Simulation mode
  At this stage, the learner begins to think in the foreign language. The language is used for inner dialogue, planning, emotions, and spontaneous perception. Reactions become increasingly automatic and immediate.
  
  5) Anticipation mode
  The brain develops a predictive readiness. It begins anticipating which structures, expressions, or grammatical patterns best fit a particular communicative purpose.
  
  6) Concept mode
  Thinking of a concept directly evokes linguistic patterns in the target language, without conscious translation. Language becomes tied to abstract thought itself.
  
  What I want to emphasize is that learning vocabulary is not merely about creating associations that “make sense.” Many language courses seem to assume that forming a simple mental link is sufficient — for example, imagining yourself walking down a creepy lane in Paris to remember a word.
  
  But what matters more than merely creating a link is attaching meaning or weight to the word. Emotional relevance appears to strengthen retention far more deeply than arbitrary association alone.
  
  The brain does not simply connect a word to an image. It connects significance to the word — in other words, the brain treats the word as important.

    ↳ **@rashidah9307** (👍1 · 2026-07-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJBP34upuAM&lc=Ugx6XV0-c6nEosHh3o54AaABAg.AWrD1H1GpoPAY2awrqJ89m
      @RafałKamiński-n8c Not flashcards the way Olly described them. But the way linguists like Language Jones described them: whole phrases or short sentences that are relevant to your life or that you learned from the context of real conversations in your target language. This is one of the most effective ways to move knowledge OF the language into the category of procedural knowledge, so that you can actually use grammar and vocabulary correctly on demand. It’s actually quite effective and it avoids all the pitfalls that he mentioned, as long as it’s done with spaced repetition. There are ideas that we all want to be able to express about our lives or about the world without waiting to find that sentence in a reader or transcript.

**@JWinch** (👍1 · 2026-08-09) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RCnw3sCyEb0&lc=UgwymxOsF9p4KkHyziV4AaABAg
  I can't speak for the general academic field, but I think the situation in AI/ML research may differ from the circumstances that led to the recommendations in this video. One of the findings in my SLR (no SLR AI usage), currently in peer review by 5 reviewers at a top 10 AI journal (Artificial Intelligence Review), is that the AI/ML field may not do systematic literature reviews often enough. I didn't even filter to PRISMA systematic literature reviews when I found ~3% of NLP papers and closer to 1% of Computer Vision papers were systematic literature reviews. Anecdotally, of this SLR's 8 nearest neighbors, only 2 used a non-ad hoc method: 1 PRISMA and 1 a method I wasn't familiar with. There are several reasons behind this, which I detail in the paper.
  
  The consequence became a main finding in the SLR: I reviewed dozens of papers claiming state of the art whose authors and reviewers seemed unaware that the state of the art had actually been reached 5 years earlier, or why. So I'm doubtful that reviewers of AI/ML papers will require all the things mentioned in the PRISMA guide, even though these authors are arguably better positioned than most to actually do them. In many other fields, authors might not be familiar with some of those terms, or know whether the AI they chose could provide them. (No diss on those authors; it's genuinely nerdy stuff that AI vendors tend to shield users from.)
  
  We're using a lot of AI on my second SLR, bridging the bleeding-edge/What Me Worry? attitude of AI/ML with a field that traditionally values PRISMA/PROSPERO (though it's not medical, which helps). But it is not making decisions; it only gives recommendations. And it does save time in many ways.
  
  Given the limited interest in lit reviews in the AI/ML field, I'm seriously considering extending the AI-enhanced SLR tools I built for my 2nd SLR and offering them to the AI/ML community, to take the biggest pain out of lit reviews so people do more of them, stop reinventing the wheel, and find actual research gaps. I believe that, at least in AI/ML, the field could benefit from more AI (applied well, using good tools like the FastTrack Claude integration you continue to enhance, thank you; what I'm building for SLRs, and what others I saw at EACL 2026 are building) to help people manage information overload, avoid repeating others' mistakes, and find useful results faster.

**@kparag01** (👍4 · 2026-07-29) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zzAFnqioNzc&lc=UgxB6yNqm17bvUNRkIZ4AaABAg
  is it secured to use through MCP ?
    ↳ **@profdavidstuckler [channel author]** (👍3 · 2026-07-29) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zzAFnqioNzc&lc=UgxB6yNqm17bvUNRkIZ4AaABAg.AZjQVTO6MPvAZjUr3k7ij_
      Yes. The connector is read-only. It only receives the search query Claude sends it, and the only thing it returns is published paper metadata (titles, abstracts, citation counts, links) from the databases. There’s no account, no login, nothing to store so it never sees your name, email, files, or anything else in your conversation. Traffic is encrypted and because requests reach us via Claude’s servers, we can’t even see your IP address, so the searches arrive effectively anonymous. The one sensible habit, as with any search engine, is to put research topics in your queries, not personal details.

**@AnotherproblemOn** (👍2 · 2026-07-31) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zzAFnqioNzc&lc=UgwO0-g-1uEeZIyoDYN4AaABAg

    ↳ **@profdavidstuckler [channel author]** (👍1 · 2026-07-31) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zzAFnqioNzc&lc=UgwO0-g-1uEeZIyoDYN4AaABAg.AZtG-AAejJAAZtOYF-Ux8-
      Super let me know what you think. Consensus is good at what it does, which is answering a question with a search. Ours does something different. It runs named methods, the Duplication Test, gap saturation, citation trajectory, inside a conversation, so you can narrow one question over ten or fifteen linked queries rather than one search at a time. And it deliberately won’t tell you your idea is good. It hands you the papers with DOIs and the method to judge them, because the judgement is the skill your examiner is testing. I built it the way I check my own topics. Use both if you like. Ours is free.
